ui.homeDescriptionLast: Discover lost works of art. Some may resurface, others are lost forever, but all cling to our memories.

ui.aboutDescription: Not Yet Forgotten (NYF) invites you to discover works of art lost throughout history. Some were stolen, others destroyed. Their images, traces and stories still allow us to encounter them.
ui.aboutInvitation: One discovery leads to another. Take time to look, to read, then to encounter a new work.

rembrandt-tempete.title: Christ in the Storm on the Sea of Galilee
rembrandt-tempete.headline: A storm. Then silence.
story: A boat, waves, a shaft of light breaking through the sky. In 1633, Rembrandt painted this biblical scene: it is his only known painted seascape.
On 18 March 1990, thieves disguised as police officers entered the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston. Thirteen works were taken. This canvas was cut from its frame.
The empty frames remain in the museum, holding a place for the missing works.

image.alt: A sailing boat in rough seas, illuminated by a break in the clouds: Christ in the Storm on the Sea of Galilee by Rembrandt.

vermeer-concert.title: The Concert
vermeer-concert.headline: Music left to the imagination.
story: Two women and a man gather around a harpsichord. One woman plays, the other sings from a score, while the man, seen from behind, plays the lute.
Isabella Stewart Gardner acquired The Concert in Paris in 1892. Almost a century later, it was among the thirteen works taken from the museum on 18 March 1990.
The reproduction still allows us to linger over this quiet gathering, while the original canvas remains missing.

image.alt: Two women and a man gathered around a harpsichord: The Concert by Johannes Vermeer.

manet-tortoni.title: Chez Tortoni
manet-tortoni.headline: An unexpected glance in a café.
story: A man in a top hat pauses and looks at us. A sketchbook and a glass sit before him: Manet captures a moment in the life of a Parisian café.
Acquired for Isabella Stewart Gardner in 1922, this small painting was stolen in March 1990. It was the only work taken from the museum’s first floor that night.
The thieves left its frame in the security director’s office. The image preserves this encounter with a stranger.

image.alt: A man wearing a top hat looks at the viewer, seated before a sketchbook in a café: Chez Tortoni by Manet.

van-gogh-tarascon.title: The Painter on the Road to Tarascon
van-gogh-tarascon.collection: Former collection of the Kaiser-Friedrich-Museum, Magdeburg
van-gogh-tarascon.headline: On the road, a shadow remains.
story: A painter walks along a sunlit road carrying his equipment. His figure and shadow stand out against the colours of the landscape. Van Gogh painted this work in 1888.
The canvas belonged to the museum in Magdeburg when it was moved to a salt mine for safekeeping during the Second World War. Its trail goes cold in 1945; it is generally considered destroyed.
Reproductions made before its disappearance still allow us to encounter this painter on his way. The exact fate of the original remains uncertain.

image.alt: A painter carrying his equipment walks along a tree-lined road, casting a long shadow: The Painter on the Road to Tarascon by Van Gogh.
image.credit: Archival reproduction · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

sourceLabels: Ōtsuka Museum — article on the reproduction

rembrandt-dame-gentilhomme.title: A Lady and Gentleman in Black
rembrandt-dame-gentilhomme.headline: Two figures in the half-light.
story: In a dark interior, a man stands beside a seated woman. Their black clothes draw attention to their faces and white collars.
Painted in 1633, this double portrait was cut from its frame in the Dutch Room during the theft of 18 March 1990.
The frame preserved at the museum marks the place of the missing canvas.

image.alt: A standing man and a seated woman dressed in black: A Lady and Gentleman in Black by Rembrandt.

rembrandt-autoportrait.title: Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
rembrandt-autoportrait.headline: A face in just a few centimetres.
story: A cap, curls and a gaze turned towards us: Rembrandt portrays himself in this tiny etching.
Acquired by Isabella Stewart Gardner in 1886, it was the first work by Rembrandt to enter her collection.
On 18 March 1990, the thieves took it from the Dutch Room. Measuring just 4.5 × 5 cm, it is one of the thirteen missing pieces.

image.alt: An etched self-portrait of the young Rembrandt wearing a cap, with long curly hair.

flinck-obelisque.title: Landscape with an Obelisk
flinck-obelisque.headline: Light on a monument
story: Beneath a clouded sky, an obelisk rises in a landscape of trees, water and tiny travellers.
Long attributed to Rembrandt, this painting of 1638 was recognised in the 1980s as the work of his pupil Govaert Flinck.
It was removed from its frame in the Dutch Room during the theft of 18 March 1990.

image.alt: A dark river landscape with trees and an illuminated obelisk: Landscape with an Obelisk by Flinck.

degas-sortie-pesage.title: Leaving the Paddock
degas-sortie-pesage.headline: The moment before the track.
story: A jockey in a red cap rides a horse seen from behind. A man leads the animal towards the track: Degas catches a moment in the preparations for a race.
The museum dates this small watercolour to the nineteenth century without specifying a year. Isabella Stewart Gardner bought it in Paris in 1919.
It is one of the five works by Degas taken from the Short Gallery on 18 March 1990.

image.alt: A jockey on a horse seen from behind, led towards the track by a man: Leaving the Paddock by Degas.

degas-cortege-florence.title: Procession on a Road near Florence
degas-cortege-florence.medium: Pencil and sepia wash on paper
degas-cortege-florence.headline: Figures following the road.
story: A pale road crosses a landscape in sepia wash. Figures and a horse-drawn cart move through this procession drawn by Degas between 1857 and 1860.
Isabella Stewart Gardner acquired this sheet in Paris in 1919 at a sale of the artist’s studio.
It was stolen from the Short Gallery with four other works by Degas on 18 March 1990.

image.alt: A procession of figures and a horse-drawn cart on a road, drawn in sepia wash by Degas.

degas-trois-jockeys.title: Three Mounted Jockeys
degas-trois-jockeys.medium: Black ink, washes and oil pigments on brown paper
degas-trois-jockeys.headline: Movement taking shape.
story: A jockey and his mount dominate the sheet. Two smaller riders, drawn upside down at the bottom, reveal Degas’s process of study.
Made around 1885–1888, the work combines ink, coloured washes and oil pigments on brown paper.
Acquired in 1919, it is one of five works by Degas stolen from the Short Gallery on 18 March 1990.

image.alt: A study of jockeys on brown paper: a large rider in profile and two others drawn upside down at the bottom.

degas-programme-96.title: Study for the Programme de la soirée artistique du 15 juin 1884 (Galerie Ponsin)
degas-programme-96.headline: An evening sketched on paper.
story: Dancers, instruments and figures surround an area filled with marks suggesting text. Degas prepares the programme for an artistic evening at Galerie Ponsin in 1884.
This sheet is catalogued as 3.1.o.96. It is distinct from the museum’s other study for the same programme.
The two drawings, acquired together in 1919, were taken from the Short Gallery on 18 March 1990.

image.alt: Degas’s study 3.1.o.96 for the Ponsin programme: dancers, instruments and a large area marked with vertical lines.

degas-programme-97.title: Study for the Programme de la soirée artistique du 15 juin 1884 (Galerie Ponsin)
degas-programme-97.headline: The same project, another sheet.
story: A dancer, instruments and figures fill this other study for the 1884 evening at Galerie Ponsin. A large rectangle at the lower right remains almost empty.
Catalogued as 3.1.o.97, this sheet is distinct from study 3.1.o.96: their dimensions and some drawn details differ.
Acquired with the other study in 1919, it also disappeared in the theft of 18 March 1990 from the Short Gallery.

image.alt: Degas’s study 3.1.o.97 for the Ponsin programme: a dancer, instruments and an almost empty rectangle at the lower right.

gu-bronze.title: Gu
gu-bronze.headline: An ancient vessel, a recent absence.
story: This ritual bronze vessel has a narrow waist, a flaring mouth and geometric decoration. It dates to the twelfth century BCE, during the Shang dynasty.
Shang elites used vessels of this type to make offerings to ancestors. Isabella Stewart Gardner acquired this gu in 1922.
Displayed in the Dutch Room, it was taken on 18 March 1990. The theft included this ancient object as well as paintings and drawings.

image.alt: A Chinese bronze gu with a flaring mouth, narrow waist and geometric decoration.

aigle-imperial.title: Eagle Finial
aigle-imperial.headline: The emblem detached from its flag.
story: An eagle with outstretched wings stands on a base marked with the number 1. This gilded bronze finial crowned the flag of the First Regiment of Grenadiers of Foot of Napoleon’s Imperial Guard.
Dated 1813–1814 and made after Chaudet and Thomire, it entered the collection with the flag in 1880.
On 18 March 1990, the thieves took the eagle from the Short Gallery. The flag remained at the museum; the archival photograph shows both before their separation.

image.alt: Black-and-white archival photograph of the eagle above its flag; only the eagle was stolen.
image.credit: Archival photograph · Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum

aigle-imperial.artist: After Antoine-Denis Chaudet and Pierre-Philippe Thomire

gardner-1990.title: The Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum theft
gardner-1990.description: On 18 March 1990, two men disguised as police officers stole thirteen pieces from the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston: five paintings, five works on paper by Degas, a Rembrandt etching and two bronze objects. All thirteen are gathered here.

tarascon-1945.title: Disappearance during the Second World War
tarascon-1945.description: The painting was moved to a salt mine for safekeeping during the Second World War. It has been missing since 1945 and is presumed destroyed. The exact circumstances remain uncertain; this record does not imply that other works disappeared in the same incident.
sourceLabels: Ōtsuka Museum — article on the reproduction
